items.description: Ash-laden winds roll in from the northern flats. Visibility drops to arm's length. Intake vents pack with frozen soot.
Particulate rain. Secondary ash columns from the eastern crater fields drift overhead for four days. Respiratory loads increase.
Cold air traps the surface layer. Smoke, particulates, and radon accumulate below the inversion ceiling. Outdoor activity becomes acutely dangerous.
Supercooled water droplets crystallize in the lower atmosphere. Roads and rooftops become mirror-slick. Patrol range halved.
The deepest blizzard of the season. Sector patrols are grounded. Supply runs to the outer ring are suspended by standing order. Caloric demand spikes sharply in the cold.
Late-freeze ashfall from the western burn perimeters. Water cisterns require extended filtration. Rooftop panels lose efficiency under the coat of grey.
Sector artillery exchanges kick pulverised rubble into the upper air column. Dust plumes drift south. Morale among shelter populations drops as the bombardment becomes audible.
Secondary particulate from collapsed structures to the north. Not the worst the season has offered, but persistent and demoralising.
The heaviest exchange of the siege phase. Continuous shelling to the north-east drives a rolling dust wall across the sector. Radon readings climb as disturbed soil vents subsurface gas.
Another inversion layer. Combat emissions compound with naturally venting radon. The scrubbers run continuously. Fuel consumption is unsustainable at this rate.
Meltwater from the plateau overwhelms the sector drainage network. Subsurface cavities collapse as permafrost liquefies. Radon liberation from the thawing ground is severe. Lower tunnels flood.
A late cold snap causes brief ice fog as refreezing melt water evaporates at the surface. Movement is hazardous on exposed slopes.

The great black-mud runoff. Every surface route is compromised. Long-wave broadcast frequencies degrade from atmospheric ionisation. This is what the Reckoning accounts referenced — the melt the machine was built to survive.
Residual ash from the last siege burns drifts south on spring thermals. A thin grey coat on the snowmelt puddles. The season is almost finished.
